title: Bisect Fundamentals
description: Use git bisect to perform a binary search through Git history and find the commit that introduced a regression.

data.text: git bisect uses a binary search algorithm to efficiently find the commit that introduced a regression. Instead of checking out every commit from the last known-good to the current broken state, bisect cuts the search space in half with each step, finding the culprit in log2(N) steps.

You provide a known-good commit and a known-bad commit. Git checks out the commit halfway between them. You test whether the bug is present, then tell Git 'good' or 'bad'. Git then narrows the range and repeats until it identifies the first bad commit.

data.title: Start and run a bisect session
data.code:
# Start bisect — known good and known bad
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
# The bug is NOT present at this commit (2 weeks ago)
git bisect good v2.1.0

# Git checks out a commit halfway between
# Test it: is the bug present?

# If bug IS present:
git bisect bad

# If bug is NOT present:
git bisect good

# Repeat until Git identifies the first bad commit

# Finish the bisect and return to HEAD
git bisect reset

data.title: Bisect is dramatically faster than manual search
data.text: For a repository with 1000 commits, a linear search requires up to 1000 checks. Bisect requires at most 10 (log2(1000) ≈ 10). For 1,000,000 commits, bisect requires at most 20 steps.

At each bisect step, you need a reliable way to determine whether the bug is present. This can be a manual test (running the app and observing behavior), an automated test, or any other reproducible check.

items: **Manual testing** — Run the app and observe the behavior
**Automated test** — Run a specific test that reproduces the bug
**Log inspection** — Check for the presence of a specific error message
**Build check** — Verify the project builds without a specific error

data.text: Git bisect maintains state in .git/BISECT_START, .git/BISECT_LOG, and .git/BISECT_NAMES. Use git bisect log to see the full search history and git bisect view to see the current bisect state.

data.title: Inspect bisect state
data.code:
# See the current bisect log
git bisect log

# View current state
git bisect visualize

# See the current bisect range
git rev-list --bisect-all main

# Abort the bisect at any time
git bisect reset

# Replay a saved bisect log
git bisect replay bisect-log.txt

# Skip a commit that cannot be tested
git bisect skip abc1234

data.text: Some commits cannot be tested — they may be broken for reasons unrelated to the bug. Use git bisect skip to tell Git to ignore that commit and continue the binary search.

data.title: Skip a commit during bisect
data.code:
# Skip a specific commit

git bisect skip abc1234

# Skip multiple commits
git bisect skip abc1234 def5678 ghi9012

# Skip the current commit
git bisect skip

items.question: Does bisect modify my working directory?
items.answer: Yes. Each step of bisect checks out a different commit. Your working directory changes with each good/bad decision. Do not have uncommitted changes when starting bisect.

items.question: Can I use bisect on a subset of commits?
items.answer: Yes. Use git bisect start <bad> <good> -- <pathspec> to limit the bisect to commits that touch a specific file or directory.

items.question: What if I accidentally skip too many commits?
items.answer: git bisect reset cancels the bisect. Restart from scratch with the correct good/bad range.

items.question: Can bisect handle merge commits?
items.answer: Yes, but merge commits can complicate the search. Use git bisect skip for commits that are difficult to test due to merge conflicts.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: git bisect performs a binary search through commit history
Provide one known-good and one known-bad commit to start
Test each step and mark as 'good' or 'bad' — bisect narrows the range
Use git bisect skip for commits that cannot be tested
git bisect reset returns to your original branch state
